title: Safer platform defaults can hold user choices, shifting online safety from individual vigilance toward interface design
source_unit: Ofcom, Protective defaults for social media platforms: Adults and Under 18s Defaults Trial
geography: United Kingdom; children aged 13-17 and adults in Ofcom randomized online mock-platform experiments

denominator.unit: Ofcom experiment participants across children aged 13-17 and adults; exact pooled denominator is reported in the technical report

settings_tested.value: sensitive-content exposure, location sharing, direct messaging, and network expansion

safety_default_retention.value: high across all age groups and setting types

mechanism.value: Platform safety can be produced through the initial choice architecture and retained settings, reducing the amount of vigilance users must supply after entering a service

observations.method: Ofcom randomized controlled trial using mock social-media platform settings with children aged 13-15, 16-17, and adults; the experiment tested safety-by-design defaults and supportive messaging across multiple controls.
observations.uncertainty: Mock online trials cannot fully reproduce real-world social norms, peer influence, platform incentives, repeated exposure, or long-run behavior; high retention in the experiment is not proof of harm reduction in live services.
observations.subgroup: Children aged 13-15, children aged 16-17, and adults, with direct age-group comparisons under the same experimental conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Participants may accept protective defaults because the experiment makes safety salient; real users may opt out when defaults reduce reach, convenience, social connection, or commercial value.

observations.period: Prior Ofcom experiments; sensitive-content and recommendation defaults

denominator.unit: participants in prior Ofcom mock-platform experiments; source page reports percentages without pooled denominator

adults_reduced_sensitive_content_when_al.unit: percent choosing reduced sensitive content when all content types was preselected

adults_reduced_sensitive_content_without.unit: percent choosing reduced sensitive content when neither option was preselected

adults_accept_reduced_sensitive_content_.unit: percent accepting reduced sensitive content when that setting was preselected

children_maintain_no_harmful_recommendat.unit: approximate percent maintaining a no-harmful-content recommendation choice when defaulted

children_maintain_choice_without_default.unit: approximate percent maintaining the no-harmful-content recommendation choice without a default

mechanism.value: Defaults change the observed distribution of safety choices, with protective preselection producing materially more acceptance or retention than neutral or permissive starting states

observations.method: Ofcom summary of prior randomized mock-platform experiments comparing permissive, neutral, and protective default settings.
observations.uncertainty: The reported percentages come from separate experiments and should not be read as one common treatment effect; the source page does not provide all sample sizes or confidence intervals.
observations.subgroup: Adults in the sensitive-content experiment and children in the harmful-recommendation experiment, as specified by the source.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher acceptance may represent passive inattention or low perceived stakes rather than informed preference; default effects may weaken when users understand the trade-offs or have strong social reasons to change settings.

denominator.unit: Ofcom trial participants and accompanying survey respondents; exact denominator is reported in the technical report

default_types.value: location sharing, direct messaging, network expansion, and sensitive-content controls

mechanism.value: User protection becomes a contest over who controls the starting state: platform design and regulation can convert stated safety support into lower-exposure defaults, while users retain an avenue to change settings

observations.method: Ofcom randomized experiment plus accompanying survey of support for safety-by-design defaults, spanning adults and under-18s.
observations.uncertainty: Support is an attitude measure and retention is an experimental behavior; neither establishes democratic legitimacy, enforceable implementation, equal effects by disability or language, or durable safety outcomes.
observations.subgroup: UK adults and children aged 13-17 included in the Ofcom research programme.
observations.counterinterpretation: Protective defaults can impose access, privacy, social, or expressive costs; a default that is safe for one user may be restrictive or exclusionary for another.

related_sources.claim: Ofcom's accompanying insights report provides the experimental design, results, and subgroup detail for protective defaults.
Ofcom's broader children’s online experiences programme provides the monitoring context for platform safety and exposure research.

boundary: This record adds Ofcom experimental evidence on safety-by-design defaults, choice architecture, and user retention of protective settings. It does not establish live-platform harm reduction, long-run user behavior, platform compliance, causal mental-health effects, or equal safety across user groups.
